title: React + TypeScript: Tab Switcher
businessContext: Build and verify the core behavior behind Tab Switcher. This independently authored exercise has a bounded, explicit contract. Injected clock, network, random, or worker models are identified in the contract; they do not claim production service guarantees.
problemStatement:
Export App({items=[{id:"one",title:"One",body:"First"},{id:"two",title:"Two",body:"Second"}]}). Render one native button per item with aria-pressed matching selection, and selected body in [data-testid="panel"]. Initially first selected; empty items show No sections. IDs are stable.

TypeScript contract: export default App and export AppProps. Use strict TSX with typed props, state, event handlers, refs and domain records. The compiler rejects implicit/explicit any and suppression directives before DOM tests or preview. Only react and react/jsx-runtime imports are supported.
constraints: Export default App. Only react and react/jsx-runtime imports are supported. The DOM contract and supplied props define the exercise.
Preserve identity, ordering, boundary behavior, and error messages stated in the contract. Passing fixtures verifies this contract, not every production concern.
Keep the supplied AppProps contract and type-safe state transitions. A passing submission must type-check and pass the original DOM journeys.
candidateTasks: Implement the documented behavior without hard-coding fixture answers.
Run the full suite, investigate boundary failures, and explain the follow-up variation.
Model the component data and narrow nullable refs and unknown errors without disabling type checking.
hints: Inspect AppProps and the inferred state type first. Fix the first compiler diagnostic before running the DOM journey.
Write down the state or algorithmic invariant, and trace the smallest boundary case before coding.
Model the active key, derive the visible content, and decide whether inactive content should remain mounted.
alternativeApproaches: Let URL state select a section and define how browser back/forward changes the active key.
commonMistakes: Ignoring contract boundaries such as: Initial key; selected tab; invalid key fallback.
Treating a local deterministic model as proof of durable storage, authorization, distributed coordination, or physical-world guarantees.
